title: The Song of Moses and of the Lamb
summary: John sees seven angels holding the seven last plagues, which complete God's wrath. Beside a sea of glass mixed with fire stand those who have conquered the beast, singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb in praise of God's just and true ways. The heavenly temple opens, the seven angels receive seven golden bowls full of God's wrath, and the temple fills with smoke from God's glory so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished.
story: Chapter 14 previewed the end, the fall of Babylon and the harvest of the earth. Chapter 15 introduces the last series of seven, the bowls, which chapter 16 will pour out. It is the shortest chapter in Revelation, and most of it is worship. Before the final judgments fall, the reader is shown the people who have come through, standing safe on the far shore and singing. The seals, trumpets, and bowls have grown steadily in scope, and the bowls are called the last because with them God's wrath is completed. The chapter frames what follows as an exodus: God's people are delivered, and the powers that enslaved them are judged.
historical:
The scene is set in heaven, but its pattern comes from Israel's founding story. After the Israelites crossed the Red Sea and saw Pharaoh's army drowned, Moses and the people sang to the LORD (Exodus 15:1-18), and Miriam led the women with tambourines. For first-century readers, the exodus was the great story of God's rescue from imperial power, remembered every year at Passover. Jews under Roman rule looked for a new exodus, and the early Christians proclaimed that it had come in Jesus. Revelation's hearers, a minority in cities devoted to the emperor, would have heard this chapter as the promise that their rescue was as certain as Israel's.

The tent of witness, or tabernacle of the Testimony, was the portable sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness, named for the tablets of the covenant law, called the Testimony, kept inside the ark (Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:7). By John's day neither tabernacle nor temple stood in Jerusalem if the book was written after AD 70, and even before that the tabernacle was a memory centuries old. John sees its true heavenly original, which Hebrews 8:5 says the earthly one copied.
cultural:
The sea of glass first appeared before the throne in 4:6. Now it is mixed with fire, and the victors stand beside it, a picture that recalls Israel standing on the shore of the Red Sea after the crossing. Their harps belong to temple worship, as in 5:8 and 14:2. The song itself is woven from Old Testament phrases rather than quoting Exodus 15 directly: God's great and wonderful works (Psalm 111:2; 139:14), his just and true ways (Deuteronomy 32:4, from the second song of Moses), the question of who will not fear the King of the nations (Jeremiah 10:7), and the promise that all nations will come and worship (Psalm 86:9).

The angels' clean, bright linen and golden sashes are priestly dress; the risen Christ wears a golden sash in 1:13. Golden bowls were used in temple service for offerings (1 Kings 7:50). Smoke filling the sanctuary so that no one could enter recalls the dedication of the tabernacle, when the glory of the LORD filled it and Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:34-35), the dedication of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11), and Isaiah's vision, where the house filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:4).
literary: Verse 1 introduces the seven angels as a great and marvelous sign, and then the chapter pauses for worship before they act (vv. 2-4), a pattern Revelation uses throughout: every series of judgments is framed by worship. The song has a clear structure of praise, question, and reasons: God's works and ways are praised; the question who will not fear you is asked; and three reasons follow, each introduced in Greek by the word for (hoti): God alone is holy, all nations will come, and his righteous acts have been revealed. Verses 5 to 8 return to the angels, who come out of the temple, receive the bowls from one of the four living creatures, and wait while the temple fills with smoke. Chapter 15 thus links the throne scene of chapter 4, with its sea and living creatures, to the final judgments.

outline.t: Seven angels with the seven last plagues
The victors sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb
The temple opened, the bowls given, the glory filling the temple

doctrines.note: The redeemed sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. The deliverance from Egypt and the deliverance through Christ are one story of rescue, and the saved stand beside the sea as those who have conquered the beast by faithfulness.

The song praises God as “Just and true” in his ways even as the last plagues are about to fall. Judgment is presented not as an embarrassment for God's people but as the revelation of his righteous acts.
The victors' song expects that all nations will come and worship before God. Even at the threshold of the last judgments, the hope of the nations' turning to God is sung, not abandoned.
The temple fills with smoke from God's glory and power, and no one can enter. God's holiness is his unapproachable majesty, and his judgments proceed from it.

words.note: Ōdē, song, a sung poem of praise. Revelation's new song (5:9; 14:3) is here identified with the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Paul uses the same word for the spiritual songs believers sing to one another (Ephesians 5:19).

Mōusēs, Moses. The only time Revelation names him. Linking Moses and the Lamb shows that the church's salvation is continuous with Israel's: the same God who brought Israel out of Egypt has acted in Christ, and his people sing one song.

Teleō, to finish or complete. With the seven last plagues God's wrath is completed, and no one can enter the temple until the plagues are completed. The same verb appears in John 19:28 as Jesus' work on the cross nears completion.

Phialē, a bowl, a shallow dish used for drinking or for offerings in worship. In 5:8 the golden bowls held incense, the prayers of the saints; here golden bowls hold God's wrath. The link suggests that the final judgments are, in part, God's answer to his people's prayers for justice.

christ: The song is the song of Moses and of the Lamb, and the pairing says who Jesus is. Moses led Israel out of slavery; the Lamb, whose blood marked the Passover pattern (5:9), leads a people from every nation out of slavery to sin and the powers of the world. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:3) and as the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). Strikingly, the song praises only God and never mentions the Lamb or the victors themselves; salvation through the Lamb leads to the worship of God. The song's hope that all nations will come and worship fulfills Psalm 86:9, a promise Christians see being answered as the gospel goes to the nations through Christ.
questions: The victors sing on the far shore before the final plagues fall. What would it look like to praise God before your own story is resolved?
The song of Moses and of the Lamb joins Israel's rescue to Christ's. How does seeing salvation as a new exodus change your understanding of what Jesus did?
The song never mentions the singers' own victory, only God's works and ways. What does that suggest about how worship should sound?
